Patient demographics:
  age: 66
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Roofer
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 36

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Olfactory (Smell): Related smells
  Maladaptive Strategies: Past Dwelling: I dwell on how I used to be before the event, Avoid Assertiveness: never disagree or assert myself to avoid conflict, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
  Memory: Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Hopelessness: I have no future, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Boon-Nam Srisawat is a 66-year-old Thai-American man who has worked as a roofer for nearly four decades, a trade he took up after immigrating to the United States in his late twenties. He lives with his wife in a modest home in a suburb of Houston, and until recently he was known among his crew as steady and capable — the kind of man who could read a roofline by feel and who rarely needed to be told something twice. That version of himself is one he now thinks about with a grief he cannot fully articulate.

Approximately fourteen months ago, Boon-Nam was part of a crew re-roofing a commercial building that had been flagged for renovation but not yet fully cleared. Without adequate warning, he and two colleagues spent the better part of a morning working in close proximity to improperly stored industrial solvents — chemicals that had been sealed behind a ventilation panel and that, when disturbed by the work above, began leaking fumes into the enclosed attic space where Boon-Nam was laying underlayment. He noticed the smell first: sharp, almost sweet, but wrong in a way he could not name. Within minutes his eyes were streaming and his chest felt as though a hand were pressing from inside. By the time he understood what was happening, he was disoriented and struggling to find the hatch he had climbed through. He remembers being on his hands and knees, unable to call out, convinced in that moment that he was dying alone in the dark and the heat, with no one who could see him. He was eventually pulled out by a colleague and transported by ambulance to a hospital, where he was treated for acute chemical inhalation. He was discharged after two days, told his lung function would likely recover, and sent home.

The recovery, however, has not followed the trajectory anyone described to him. In the weeks after the incident, Boon-Nam began waking in the night, sometimes in complete darkness, and finding himself back in that attic — not remembering it, but inhabiting it, his chest tight, his body certain that the air was wrong. His memories of the event are extraordinarily vivid, detailed in ways that feel almost photographic: the particular grain of the plywood beneath his palms, the quality of the light through the gap in the eaves. These memories arrive without invitation, replaying with a completeness that exhausts him. There are also moments when the emotional weight of the event descends without any accompanying image — a sudden wave of dread or helplessness that he cannot locate or explain, which leaves him feeling as though something is happening to him that he cannot control or predict.

Smell has become a source of particular vigilance. When his wife uses certain cleaning products in the house, Boon-Nam leaves the room without explanation. A visit to his physician last spring — the antiseptic smell of the waiting room — sent him into a state of rigid, silent distress that he managed by sitting near the exit and focusing on the floor. He has not told his doctor about this. He has not told his wife the full extent of what he experiences, partly because he has come to believe that disagreeing or asserting himself in any conversation risks something he cannot afford to lose, and so he has learned to say little and concede much. He tries, with considerable effort, to not think about the event at all, and yet the effort itself seems to keep him tethered to it.

He no longer takes jobs that involve enclosed or unfamiliar structures. He has turned down work that would have paid well, offering his foreman vague explanations. He cannot fully relax even sitting in his own living room, and his concentration — once reliable, once a point of quiet professional pride — has become unreliable in ways that shame him. He finds himself dwelling on who he was before: a man who could trust his own body and his own judgment. He has come to feel that he cannot rely on that man anymore, that the world contains dangers that do not announce themselves, and that his future has a quality of foreclosure he cannot see past.

What finally brought him to seek help was his wife asking him, quietly, whether he was still there. He did not know how to answer her. He is hoping, tentatively, that someone can tell him whether he can come back. What he fears most is that the answer is no.
